difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing amortized cost from the worst-case cost of a single operation, a common point of confusion in interviews.
prompt: A backend service appends items one at a time to a dynamic array that starts empty and doubles its capacity whenever it becomes full. Across a long sequence of N appends, what is the amortized time complexity of a single append, and why?
explanation: Doubling means the total work spent copying elements during all resizes across N appends sums to O(N) (a geometric series dominated by the last resize), so that total cost spread evenly across the N appends is O(1) per append on average, even though any single append that triggers a resize costs O(n) by itself.

options.text: O(1) amortized, because the total cost of all the periodic O(n) resizes across N appends sums to O(N), which averages to O(1) per append.
options.explanation: Correct: the geometric growth of capacity means the copying work across all resizes totals O(N), so dividing by N appends gives O(1) amortized per append.

options.text: O(n) amortized, because every append must first check whether the array is full before deciding to resize.
options.explanation: Checking current size against capacity is itself an O(1) comparison; it does not make the amortized cost of append O(n). This confuses a cheap bookkeeping check with the cost of the rare resize itself.

options.text: O(log n) amortized, because doubling the capacity creates a logarithmic number of resize events over the sequence.
options.explanation: There are indeed about log2(N) resize events, but their individual costs (1, 2, 4, 8, ... elements copied) sum to O(N) total, not O(log n) total — the amortized-per-append figure is O(1), not O(log n).

options.text: O(n), because any single append that triggers a resize costs O(n), and the amortized bound can never be better than the worst single operation.
options.explanation: This is the key misconception: amortized analysis spreads the occasional expensive operation's cost over the many cheap operations that preceded it, so the amortized bound is explicitly allowed to be better than the worst single-operation cost.
